title: Breadth, length, depth, height (Ephesians 3:14–21)
hookLine: Paul kneels and prays they grasp love that passes knowledge
carry: more than we ask or think
tomorrow: Paul's first rule for being one isn't a belief. what is it?

cards: At one church everyone kneels for the prayers. Across town, everyone stays on their feet. Bodies pray in different shapes.

Paul, calling himself a prisoner, writes: "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." But in Mark's Gospel Jesus says, "when ye stand praying, forgive." So which is it, kneel or stand?
Christians have practiced both, and made a case for both.

teach.h: KNEEL: HE KNEELED DOWN, AND PRAYED.
teach.b: The case for kneeling: Paul bows his knees, and Luke says Jesus in the garden "kneeled down, and prayed." Kneeling says with the whole body: I am small, you are great, please.
The case for standing: Jesus speaks of standing to pray, and here's one to tell a friend: the early church council at Nicaea asked Christians to pray standing on Sundays and in the days after Easter.
Standing, on that view, is the posture of people raised up with Christ. Some churches still keep that custom. Both sides pray to the same Father.

Then listen to what Paul asks for, on his knees. That they'd be "strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man." That Christ would live in their hearts, and they'd be rooted and grounded in love.
And that they'd "comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height." Breadth of what? He doesn't say.
The next line fills it in: "to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge." Known, truly, and never measured to the edge. And with all saints: nobody measures it alone.

teach.h: MORE THAN WE ASK OR THINK.
teach.b: Then Paul runs out of requests and breaks into praise: "Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think." Kneeling or standing, that's where the prayer lands.

how: Christians pray kneeling, standing, sitting or bowing, and churches differ: some kneel for much of their worship, while some keep the old custom of standing to pray on Sundays.

o: the width of a love too wide to measure
how far a prayer travels before God hears
the size of the city of heaven in Revelation

games.q: two postures, one prayer — tap the pairs.
p: a love known but never measured

s: the Bible commands one posture for prayer
a common assumption. Paul bows his knees; Jesus speaks of when ye stand praying.
Paul says exactly what the breadth and length belong to
he leaves it open; the next line: the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge.
Paul says this love is grasped with all saints, together
comprehend with all saints: nobody measures it alone.

games.q: your church always kneels to pray. a friend's church stands. she asks you to state the standing side at its best. which is it?
o: Jesus said when ye stand praying, and early Christians stood on Sundays as people raised with Christ.
standing is more comfortable, so people can pray for longer.
kneeling was forbidden in the Bible after Paul's time.
games.why: Mark 11:25 and the council of Nicaea's Sunday custom make the standing case; Ephesians 3:14 and Luke 22:41 make the kneeling one. both pray to the same Father.

practice: Choose a posture for this sit: kneel if your body allows, stand, or simply bow your head where you are. Notice what the posture says before you say anything.
If you pray, let Paul's line be the whole prayer: exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think.

wordCard.voice: Breadth. The first of Paul's four directions, for a love too wide to measure alone.

orig.note: Greek: breadth, width. The first of the four directions in Ephesians 3:18.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: more than we ask or think, prayed on his knees by a prisoner. Good night.
